content.confidence: 5: You are absolutely certain about your assessment. You are very familiar with the related work and checked the math/other details carefully.
content.summary_of_the_paper: This paper proposes to improve the summarization quality of the doctor-patient dialogue, so that the summary does not miss any important medical terms. By introducing new concepts such as high utilization concepts and utilization rate based on word counting, the paper proposes a reasonable regularization method for seq2seq decoding. Using a automatically generated dialogue-summary pair dataset, the paper shows the superior performance of the proposed method compared to simple baselines.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strengths:
- The entire paper is a pleasure to read. The description of the problem setting is clear, and the new concepts (high utilization concepts, utilization rate) intuitively make sense, although they are based on simple word counting.
- Solving the proposed problem can have a meaningful impact in the healthcare domain, as manually summarizing the doctor-patient dialogue is labor intensive.

Weaknesses:
- The entire dataset (train, validation, test) is constructed via labels derived from a pre-trained model, (i.e. sentence-based cosine similarity between a source sentence and a reference sentence is used to derive a sentence-wise paired dataset) which makes the whole dataset untrustworthy. The authors did not reveal which pre-trained model they used to derive the sentence-based embedding, but I'm assuming it was BERT or some BERT variant. Note that BERTscore itself is not completely reliable, and needless to say, BERTscore applied to medical corpus would make things worse. 
- The dataset is not publicly available, and the authors do not plan to open-source it either. This severely hurts the reproducibility of this work, and the readers have no option but to blindly trust the paper. Given that BERTscore was used to construct the entire dataset, the authors should open source the dataset with proper deidentification in order to pursuade the readers of the quality of the dataset.
- If labeling the entire dataset is too labor-intensive, at least there should be a sizeable amount of test set that is manually labeled by the medical experts to ensure the trustworthyness of the model's test performance. This was how ChestImaGenome was constructed.
- All evaluation metrics except "medical experts evaluation" are unreliable, as they either rely on low-resolution approximation of utilization rate (Eq.7) or metrics induced from pre-trained models such as BERT or GPT-2, which are not well-suited for evaluating the semantic quality of highly specific domains such as medicine. The entire experimental evaluation is standing on weak grounds.
- Even the user study itself is not completely reliable as the detailed process as to how the study was conducted is not explained. For example, the seq2seq model is trained to accept a source sentence (i.e. a single speech of the provider in a dialogue), then generate a reference sentence (i.e. a single care plan). But during the user study, it seems that the model is given the entire dialogue to generate any part of the care plan (e.g. medication plan or instruction).
- The baseline can be stronger than using a naive DBA proposed back in 2018, as there is a long line of research in lexically constrained decoding other than DBA.
- In Eq.3, \sum( p(v | y_{<t}) p(y_{<t}) ) equals p(v), not p(v | x). Why is it okay to ignore the condition x when calculating p(v | x)?
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
Clarity: The paper is extremely well-written, and it was a pleasure to read.

Quality: The dataset construction, experiment setup, evaluation scheme, and results analysis are all far from rigorous.

Reproducibility: The paper uses private data, with in-house tools. There is practially zero reproducibility.
content.summary_of_the_review: The problem proposed by the paper is practical and meaningful, and the approach to solving the problem, although not sophisticated, is reasonable enough. But everything else falls short. The dataset construction relies on pre-trained model, failiing the guarantee its quality, and the evaluation metrics seem to have been chosen out of convenience, rather than rigor. Overall, it is a paper with interesting ideas with a very weak follow-through. I suggest the authors take the material at hand and significantly improve the experimental rigor (perhaps open-source the dataset as well), which will make the paper much more impactful.
content.correctness: 2: Several of the paper’s claims are incorrect or not well-supported.
content.technical_novelty_and_significance: 2: The contributions are only marginally significant or novel.
content.empirical_novelty_and_significance: 1: The contributions are neither significant nor novel.

content.summary_of_the_paper: This paper focused on a very important problem in clinical text generation, factual correctness.  It tried to induce high utilization concepts by mapping text with medical concepts and restricted the lexicon when generating clinical text.
content.strength_and_weaknesses: The problem this paper focused on is very important. The proposed model is intuitive and simple, although this work only tried to improve a small problem of factual correctness by uplifting medical terms in text generation. The methodology is a traditional framework with a lexicon limit setting. The expert evaluation improves the persuasive of this paper. While the annotation details (agreement within experts, expert background) is not clear.
content.summary_of_the_review: Important problem and good manual evaluation. But the methodology has limited novelty.

content.confidence: 4: You are confident in your assessment, but not absolutely certain. It is unlikely, but not impossible, that you did not understand some parts of the submission or that you are unfamiliar with some pieces of related work.
content.summary_of_the_paper: This paper presents an approach to tackle a real problem of generating rare concepts in sequence to sequence models. The idea is simple, and relies on establishing equivalency classes using external information (such as a list of drug names). Then they can compute an utilization rate using this information to get normalized scores for each concept, and loss is augmented using the utilization rate.
content.strength_and_weaknesses: This is a straightforward yet effective approach, maybe more suitable for a workshop paper. It reads as an ad-hoc method, and it is also a common practice to use gazetteers and lists of entities in conventional NLP. A bigger challenge would be augmenting this information using a model, such as a named entity tagger with this list. For example, this approach will not work with city names or song names since every other ngram would be a hit.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib: The paper is very clear. The approach is novel and reproducible. The authors will also be making the source code available for public.
content.summary_of_the_review: It is a neat idea for exploiting the external knowledge for language generation, and authors have a nice representative task in hand. The results are convincing, and the method effective. However, I am not sure whether the paper sums up to be an ICLR paper: the approach does not scale to many other real world scenarios, and as implemented in the paper, it is almost like an ad-hoc approach, and can be improved for open class entities.
content.correctness: 4: All of the claims and statements are well-supported and correct.
